The reason is scope rather than error: this entry began as a naming convention, absorbed version agreement, then absorbed the question of whether a version belongs in identity at all, then the question of how identity reaches an artifact — four problems on one id, with 27 decisions and six reversals among them. The split follows the repo boundary and the sequencing boundary: 0010 owns what identity IS and how it reaches the artifact's bytes (a breaking core change that can be accepted without answering registry credentials), 0011 owns the commands that write it and the registry it goes to (a cli feature that depends on 0010). Both successors carry fresh decision logs starting at D1 with only current answers, and the evidence this entry gathered is restated inline there and dated rather than cross-referenced, so neither successor requires reading this one. | [0010](./0010/) | core | draft | major | not-started | 2026-07-27 — D4 REVERSED by D13; D14 and D15 recorded; the sole blocking question dissolved. Primitive FQNs keep the FULL SemVer of the build they came from (path/name@1.2.0, the form core already carries) rather than becoming major-keyed, and the `v` stays only on the module path so an ADDRESS (@v1) and a KEY (@1.2.0) never look alike. Cross-minor compatibility — the capability D4 existed to deliver — is supplied by SUBSCRIPTION BREADTH instead: a platform subscribed to a catalog major materializes every published build in it, so the composed map is the union of those key spaces and each module matches the exact build it was authored against. WHAT CHANGED THE DECISION is that the machinery already exists and D4 would have broken it: filter.go:43-100 returns EVERY survivor of a filter, materialize.go:87-95 pulls each as its own build, and index.go:57-64 documents the invariant it depends on — distinct versions yield distinct FQNs — while calling the collapse path `largely defensive`. That comment is true under SemVer keys and FALSE under D4, where every survivor of a range collides on every FQN and any changed transformer becomes `transformer %q diverges across selected builds`. The e2e failure in 01-problem is accordingly re-diagnosed: a subscription that did not cover the authored-against build, not a keying defect, and 01-problem now says so. THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDED IT, absent from the entry until now, is reproducibility: under D4 every installed module keys to @vN, so publishing catalog 1.3.0 changes the transformer bodies every installed module renders against with nobody editing a module — under SemVer keys a catalog release is inert until a module is rebuilt. It also degrades better under the one failure OPM cannot control, since a publisher who breaks compatibility inside a major poisons every installed module at once under D4 and only later-built modules under D13. Recorded plainly: core/src/types.cue:41-44 shows FQNs were already lifted major→SemVer under 0001 D5 for this reason, D4 reverted it, and D13 reverts it back — so the entry now states which failure it prefers rather than flipping again. CONSEQUENCES: D3's floor and D12's lookup are retired (nothing to compare when a key names its own build); #CatalogFloor, #SemverTriple and #VersionGTE are deleted from schemas/target.cue and #PrimitiveDemand becomes exact-key containment plus an `availableVersions` set computed by splitting the version off the demanded FQN — which makes the diagnostic BETTER (it names the demanded build and the ones materialized) and independent of OQ3. D14 changes filterVersions' empty-filter default from highestStable to every published build in the subscription key's major, which D1's @vN-bearing #registry key makes the literal reading of the key. D15 adds an explicit prerelease opt-in to #SubscriptionFilter, measured as necessary rather than tidy: catalogs/opm publishes only v1.0.0-alpha* and catalogs/kubernetes carries v1.1.0-alpha (registry read 2026-07-27), so a bare subscription gets one build and `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0` selects ZERO. OQ2 and OQ5 are dissolved rather than answered — the floor they concerned no longer exists and prerelease/0.x builds no longer share a key space — OQ5 having been the entry's only blocking question; OQ3 narrows to diagnostics quality since the lookup that could misreport is gone; OQ6 RE-OPENS, because D12 was its answer and the version is now derivable from the fqn that interpolates it. New: OQ7 (nothing prunes a monotonically-growing materialized set; deferred by agreement, and answerable because fleet demand is enumerable) and OQ8 (a moved-ahead dev checkout supplies keys that look published — OQ2's residue). New risks recorded for a narrowed subscription, unbounded build growth, and the prerelease exclusion; the shared-resolution risk is RESTATED AS WORSE — under D13 a merged module/platform resolution makes a module demand the platform's build, which the platform supplies, so it matches silently against a definition it was never authored on. New drawback: with the version back in the FQN, an open Version leaves the whole key space non-concrete, so D6's `every FQN still evaluates in an unfilled tree` no longer holds. | Module and Catalog Identity |
| [0011](./0011/) | cli | draft | minor | not-started | 2026-07-26 — Initial design recorded as D1-D7 with six open questions. The entry defines how an OPM artifact reaches a registry: one publish pipeline serving two artifact types (D1), which DERIVES its coordinates from the artifact and never rewrites the artifact to fit a coordinate (D2); version authoring split from version publishing, so a commit can sit between deciding a version and pushing one (D3); a refusal to publish an artifact whose identity is not concrete, closing the measured gap that `cue mod publish` will happily push a tree with unfilled identity fields (D4); a central registry that HOSTS rather than indexes, with owner-scoped module paths under reserved namespace segments (D5); and a local-override gate that never honours cue.mod/local-module.cue, with an explicit escape hatch for modules and none at all for catalogs, because a catalog's divergence propagates into the key space of everything built against it (D6). The four questions that block promotion are the ones this entry cannot answer from inside itself: publishing credentials, tag immutability, what replaces the modules repo's checksum-driven bump, and how the published fleet moves to the owner-scoped namespace. | Module and Catalog Publishing |

## Status legend

- **draft** — initial design, actively being written
- **accepted** — design agreed upon, ready for implementation
- **implemented** — design has been realized in code
- **superseded** — replaced by a newer enhancement (see `superseded_by` in the entry's config.yaml)
